description:
Sponsor: Get 10% off Squarespace purchases (https://geni.us/BqEpf)
This is our first Intel Arc GPU benchmark & review (other than the DG1) for a true gaming desktop video card from Intel. The Arc A380 competes with the AMD RX 6400 closest, maybe the GT 1630 (we'll see), and aims to be a $130-$150 card. The A380 launched only in China at first, but will very likely find its way into the rest of the world's markets. The Intel Arc A750 is coming next, and we have shots of that in this video, but we don't have a price target on it yet. These cards also have AV1 capabilities, which is something we'll look at in a future piece!

Watch our Intel Arc A750 hands-on & preview here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AN8ZAf15DrM
Watch our Intel A380 Tear-Down! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qoR0J9NTJyY
Watch our deep-dive on frame rendering and some info on Intel Smooth Sync: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8ENCV4xUjj0

comments.text: Unfortunately, on official benchmarking test sites, the Intel A380 is ranked in the same range as the GTX 750ti. Unless you have a computer with PCIe 4.0, at least 6 cores and 12 threads, with Re-bar hardware and software support, then your overall results and efficiency with the video card will be horrendous, and video cards more than 5 years older will outperform the A380 on much older computers.

So, I don't know if someone will still see this. But the first A380's are now starting to appear to be available 'somewhat local'. They are on reputable web shops with prices, but still 'awaiting stock'. They are listed for around 165,- to 175,- EUR. I've been looking, the only cards available NEW for less than that, are a few rx550's and rx560's,  and a single rx6400. For just slightly MORE than that, you get a 1050ti. Most of the rx6400's and 1650's start around 200,- EUR here. So the A380 appears to be quite  a bit cheaper, so performs very nicely for the price. Not saying you should get it, not at all! But for a low-end part, the performance (even with the bad performing titles taking into account) is actually quite good for the price. The cheapest RX6500 (non XT) I see is for 200,- EUR (and quickly goes up). But for that price, the RX6500 is a good buy, of course. But if I had to choose between a 1650 / 1050ti / RX6400 or pay less for an A380... it might consider the intel one and hope the drivers get better.
If this holds true for the midrange cards, I'm more interested than a few weeks ago.

Those Lows in SOTTR are amazing! From the average it only drops ~14% and then another 3-4% for the 0.1% lows! All other cards in the SOTTR benchmark dropped much further for both measurements. If one of Intel's higher end ARCs can place in the ballpark (of average framerate and pricing) of the RX 6600 or 3060 Ti we might be looking at a 140 fps AVERAGE card that has 120 fps 1% lows compared to the 3060 Ti's 112 fps 1% lows. And the 0.1% lows would be even better. The 3060 Ti drops to 95 fps at times while the hypothetical ARC would stay above 115 fps at all times. There are mixed results in the other games but it's clear that ARC does better the newer / more modern an engine is, and with higher resolutions. That's a forgivable problem to have. Nobody needs a dinosaur that chews through GTA 5 and then struggles with Cyberpunk or SOTTR.
While I can't see an argument for anyone to buy the 380 as it's just too weak to serve as an upgrade for anybody, its tendencies leave me hopeful for the higher end variants and the next generation (ARC B).

comments.text: I have been building systems upwards of 20 years or so. Generally cards that have been mined on are USUALLY okay to buy. Most Miners are like enthusiasts when it comes to voltage and temps, yes they are preforming a different task but as long as the bios has not been fubbed around with and they have taken care of their cards, you can find some killer deals out there. Plus, even cards that are not good for mining are flooding the market, so use some common sense and you can find several good deals. I have bought over roughly 50 GPUs in the last year and only 2 of them were bad and neither were advertised as previous miners, they both came from "e waste recycling" companies that really don't bother to check their stuff. One of the cards was thrown in a box, no bubble wrap no rappers no anti-static bag nothing, just chucked into a USPS flat rate box and mailed out with absolutely nothing to protect it. I'm nearly positive the seller new it was garbage and didn't pack it properly because it did not make any difference. Check the accuracy of the listing, if there's a ton of mistakes on the specs of the card, steer clear from that listing. If there is only 1 or so contact the seller and see if they can offer the correct specs. Usually sellers that list specs incorrectly do not know enough about tech or said item to fully benchmark it and give you any kind of guarantee. Also., If you get a used GPU through eBay stress the  fu€k out of it for a couple of days before you get comfortable with it. There are a lot of folks that  half ass rig and oven toast their broken GPUs and then flip them on eBay. Usually you can get a card like this to fail by running a stress test and leaving it on for a few hours. Once it blue screens you know it's screwed.

I know it's not your usual fare, but any chance of any testing under Linux? I'm only asking because Intel's Linux drivers are a huge step up from their Windows drivers not just in terms of performance, but also quality to the point where some of their iGPUs support newer versions of OpenGL or the like under Linux (eg. Sandy Bridge and Ivy Bridge: OpenGL 4.2 under Windows, 4.5 under Linux) and I wonder if the driver issues will be less prevalent there.

There's precedent for this too when you consider the Linux driver situation for AMD vs nVidia under Linux, where the open source drivers generally being faster under Vulkan than AMDs drivers on the same card combined with the proliferation of DXVK for Linux gaming (ie. Most titles are running under Vulkan for Linux) mean AMD tends to compare better than it does under Windows which makes some GPUs fare better than they otherwise would.

I'm not sure if you're paying for subtitles or not, but I'll mention this since youtube claims it's not auto-generated: the subtitles are missing quite a few of the card titles and other such technical details.  For example:
at 3:53 - "being the A7 50, an unknown prize and probably an AA 770 or similar"
at 3:56 - "The Alchemist GP is currently launching including the Acme"  (subtitle breaks in the middle of the board name, which is generally bad for subtitling, also gets "Acme"" instead of ACM-G...)
at 3:58 - "ten and the ACG 11 detailed in the slide."  (ten being from the board mentioned above, the ACM-G10

Etc.  
It's not completely incomprehensible, but here's the autogenerated subtitles for the same segments: 
"...being the a750 at an unknown price and probably an a70 or similar the alchemist gpus currently launching include the acm g10 and the acm acmg-11 detailed in this slide..."  
As you can see, autogenerated has literally no concept of punctuation and makes a couple of mistakes (a70 should be a770 to my ear, and the acm acmg-11 pulled an extra acm out of nowhere), but it's generally actually closer to what you're saying than the not autogenerated subtitles.

Which means, if you're paying for professional subtitling services, you're getting ripped off.  And if you're doing them in house, you might want to email the person doing them your script.

Something which might be interesting in regard to transients is considering people who intend to build fully passive machines, as 75w TDP is within scope for fully passive builds(db4a gpu addon, for example). It's a rare thing, but it's a consideration, particularly with the quite limited total power budgets which are reasonable to consider for minimization of coil whine.(160w and lower PSUs would be common, although 240w probably if you're putting a GPU in there anyway)

The A380 could be interesting for that in the future as Intel makes, frankly, a mature product. This is a cool first showing, and it's clearly a first showing. Once they get their software up to snuff this seems like a line worthy of at least some optimism.

As others noted, the hardware encoding in particular has always been an Intel strong point. In theory, you could get something like a ryzen pro 5650g and an A380 and have a quite respectable streaming box at extremely low power budget, for example, which may matter if you're already slamming the breaker with the kind of equipment a decked out streamer setup would otherwise have.

comments.text:
The only avenue that the A380 could have used to give itself a leg up in the market was as a cheap upgrade for older PCs, but the ReBAR requirement kills that possibility stone dead. So what we're left with is a card that has zero compelling advantages against its competitors; being better built doesn't matter one iota at this price point, and the fact that Intel is paying money for build quality suggests (a) they don't understand the market (b) they're subsidising this card. Since Intel hates losing money, with a passion, that implies they won't subsidise it for long, which won't give Arc enough time to gain decent marketshare, which means it will be dead after one generation - just like i740 and Larrabee. (Battlemage doesn't count, Intel can and will easily kill that if Arc fails.)

Ultimately, this card - and Arc as a whole - is almost certainly DOA. And as such, not recommending against it is both bizarre and contrary to what I've come to expect from GN. How can you honestly call the 6400 a turd, yet give this GPU a grudging pass?

Rumour is that one can speed up those cards by disabling AGP texturing, which makes it perform a bit faster than it normally would.

Intel if they were smart could take an approach similar to what AMD used to do years ago, where you could have the GPU pair up with onboard graphics of their APU's back then they called "Dual Graphics" if anyone is old enough to remember. Imagine if you could do this with intel and their CPU's that already had unique tech like quicksync encoding, pair that with their GPU AV1 encoding where you could pair your intel CPU + intel GPU together to make for one hell of an encoding stream beast. You could also have a situation where they could design their encoding to use the E cores on a processor to be dedicated for the combined encoding, leaving the P cores open for a game or whatever other primary program when encoding and streaming making for a possible build that has an intel GPU in a lower slot as a dedicated encoder GPU card with your main "gaming" card for the main use, having a stream/gaming rig all in one that would be able to stream encode at AV1 level for much higher quality.

comments.text: The large stutters caused by disabling ReBAR may well be caused by lack of maturity from drivers. With ReBAR, memory transfer to the GPU can be trivially implemented, since you can just map the chunk of memory you allocated and transfer to it directly. Without it, you have to figure out how to best use the 256MB of addressable space you've got available, without consuming it all since other applications will need to use the same chunk of memory. It's a very difficult conundrum and has likely taken years for both AMD and Nvidia to arrive at an acceptable solution.

comments.text:
@edwardtan1354  The problem with GPUs on a Raspberry Pi isn't just BAR space, it's that the PCIe controller refuses to allow mapping in memory from an external device. The Apple M1 has the same limitation. All modern graphics code expects to be able to directly allocate and use GPU memory as if it were CPU memory; if you can't do this then you have to do a lot of unreliable, performance-sapping workarounds.

I imagine Nvidia and AMD's drivers are already optimized around the 256MB limit and that's why they don't really get a huge boost from ReBAR. Intel likely designed everything around having unified memory access and didn't optimize the fallback case. So it could be the case that it does a bunch of extra copies or something. But without access to both Nvidia/AMD and Intel driver code we will never know.
